::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false" title="Purpose"}
This assignment helps you turn descriptive statistics and visuals into a story
that someone can act on.

You will propose five candidate project stories and create a feasible analysis
plan for each one. Your group will use these plans to select and combine its
strongest ideas.
:::

## Objectives

By the end of this assignment, you will be able to:

- write takeaway-first headlines rather than topics;
- identify relationships and the variables needed to investigate them;
- distinguish existing, derived, and external variables;
- draft testable hypotheses; and
- plan analyses and visuals that support a business story.

## Resources

- The course `.csv` extract in the `data` folder that matches your project
  domain
- Homework 2 tables and Homework 3 visuals
- Week 4 readings and slides on telling stories with data

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal" icon="false" title="Expectations"}
This is planning, not execution. Bullets and concise notes are appropriate. Your
ideas must be clear, testable, and feasible, or explicitly identify the data
that would make them feasible.
:::

## 2) Review the Headline Standard

A strong headline is a complete sentence that states a potential takeaway. It
does not need numbers or test statistics at this planning stage.

**Strong examples:**

- Chicago crashes are more likely to involve injuries under some road and
  lighting conditions.
- Late Olist deliveries receive lower review scores than on-time deliveries.
- Reminder use and scheduling lead time are related to synthetic appointment
  no-shows.

**Weak examples:**

- Crash injuries and lighting
- Olist delivery and reviews
- Appointment no-shows

The weak examples name topics but do not state a takeaway someone could evaluate.

---

## 3) Use the Analysis-Plan Structure

For every story, provide:

1. **Headline:** A complete takeaway sentence.
2. **Three relationships:** Comparisons or patterns that could support or
   challenge the headline.
3. **Variables:** Label each variable as **Exists**, **Derived**, or **External**.
4. **3-second version:** No more than 7 words and no numbers.
5. **30-second version:** 1-2 sentences stating the takeaway, who should care,
   and why.
6. **At least two hypotheses:** Testable statements.
7. **Data requirements and gaps:** Missingness, outliers, derived fields,
   external sources, and join keys.
8. **Planned analyses:** Appropriate descriptive or inferential methods.
9. **Planned visual:** A chart type and the comparison it will show.

### Worked Example

**Headline:** Chicago crashes are more likely to involve injuries under some
road and lighting conditions.

**Relationships:** Injury proportion by lighting condition; injury proportion
by road surface; median injury count by time period.

**Variables:** Injuries total (**Exists**); lighting condition (**Exists**);
road surface (**Exists**); any-injury indicator (**Derived**); traffic volume
by location (**External**).

**3-second version:** Crash injury risk varies by conditions.

**30-second version:** Chicago transportation planners should compare injury
patterns across lighting and road conditions to identify where safety responses
may deserve closer investigation.

**Hypotheses:** The proportion of crashes involving injuries differs by lighting
condition. Injury counts differ across reported road-surface conditions.

**Data requirements and gaps:** Define the injury indicator; review missing
lighting and road-surface values; obtain compatible traffic-volume data before
describing crash rates.

**Planned analyses:** Group summaries, proportion comparisons, chi-square test,
and ANOVA or a nonparametric comparison.

**Planned visual:** A sorted bar chart of injury proportions by lighting
condition.

## Submission

Submit `Homework_04_IP.pdf` in Canvas. It must contain all five completed story
plans and your top-three ranking. Keep the PDF available for the in-class group
discussion.

## Checklist

- [ ] I wrote five headlines as takeaways rather than topics.
- [ ] Every headline has three supporting relationships.
- [ ] I labeled variables as Exists, Derived, or External.
- [ ] I completed every analysis-plan component for all five stories.
- [ ] I identified data gaps or joins where needed.
- [ ] I ranked my top three stories and can present the strongest one.
- [ ] I reviewed and submitted `Homework_04_IP.pdf`.

**Grading focus:** Your work will be evaluated for takeaway-first writing,
logical relationships, feasible data requirements, testable hypotheses, and a
clear connection between each story, analysis, and visual.
